definition: Cache memory is a small-sized type of volatile computer memory that provides high-speed data storage and access to the processor and stores frequently used data and instructions.
details: Cache memory is a small-sized type of volatile computer memory that provides high-speed data storage and access to the processor and stores frequently used data and instructions.

explainer.lead: Cache memory is a small, fast holding area close to a processor for data and instructions it is likely to need again. It saves trips to slower memory, so programs can spend less time waiting.

tiers.eli5: Imagine doing homework with a huge bookcase across the room and a tiny shelf beside your desk. You keep the books you use most on the small shelf so you can grab them quickly. Cache memory does that for a computer, keeping useful information nearby instead of fetching it from slower memory every time.
tiers.practitioner: CPU caches exploit temporal and spatial locality, so data layout and repeated access patterns strongly affect hit rate and latency. Write-back caches reduce immediate backing-store writes but add dirty-data tracking and eviction costs, while write-through caches update both stores synchronously. Watch for stale copies across caches, costly misses, and replacement or prefetching choices that do not match the workload.
tiers.paperLevel: A cache is a pool of entries (tag, data), where each entry copies data from a backing store and its tag identifies that data; hit rate H = cache hits / total accesses. A miss requires a more expensive backing-store access, usually followed by insertion into the cache and possible eviction under a replacement policy. Effectiveness is bounded by the capacity–speed trade-off and workload locality, and multiple cached copies require coherence mechanisms to prevent stale data.

explainer.example: Suppose a CPU requests data whose tag is absent from its L1 cache: that is a miss, so the data is fetched through the memory hierarchy and copied into the cache. If the CPU requests the same data again before it is evicted, the matching tag produces a hit and avoids another trip to slower main memory.

usedIn.name: CPUs
usedIn.detail: Small caches on or near the processor hold instructions and data, often in cascaded levels.

usedIn.name: GPUs
usedIn.detail: Texture and other caches support graphics and general-purpose computation.

usedIn.name: Disk and solid-state drives
usedIn.detail: Hardware caches reduce access latency and can combine small transfers into larger requests.

usedIn.name: Web browsers and servers
usedIn.detail: Software caches keep copies of requested content so later requests can be answered faster.

explainer.intuition: Keeping a small supply of likely-to-be-reused information close at hand is often faster than maintaining only a much larger, slower store. This works because programs commonly reuse recent data and access data stored near previous requests.
howItWorks: A client such as a CPU first checks the cache for a tag matching the requested data.
On a hit, the cached copy is returned without consulting the slower backing store.
On a miss, the data is retrieved from the backing store and usually copied into the cache.
If space is needed, a replacement policy such as least recently used selects an entry to evict.
A write policy controls when changes reach the backing store.
explainer.whyItMatters: Caching bridges the gap between fast processors and larger, slower storage, improving latency and often throughput. Its small size keeps it cost-effective, while locality allows many requests to be served without reaching the backing store.
misconceptions: A cache miss does not mean the data is lost; it means the data must be fetched from the backing store.
A bigger cache is not automatically better, because capacity and speed involve a design trade-off.
Cache memory is temporary working storage, not a permanent place to keep files.

nodes.label: CPU request
nodes.note: Requests data from a backing-store location.

nodes.label: Cache lookup
nodes.note: Compares the request with cached entry tags.

nodes.label: Cached data
nodes.note: A matching tag produces a fast cache hit.

nodes.label: Backing store
nodes.note: Slower memory supplies data after a miss.

nodes.label: Cache fill
nodes.note: Retrieved data is copied into the cache.

nodes.label: Replacement policy
nodes.note: Chooses an existing entry to evict when space is needed.

diagram.caption: A request is answered directly on a cache hit; on a miss, data comes from the backing store and is usually cached for future requests.
